name: Mexenone

lead: Mexenone (benzophenone-10) is a UV-absorbing sunscreen filter related to oxybenzone. The appearance payoff is less cumulative sun damage, which is what drives wrinkling, rough texture and uneven tone over the years.

It absorbs ultraviolet light through its benzophenone structure, so less reaches skin cells. Most of what has been published on it comes from dermatology clinics: patch-test series from the 1980s and 1990s repeatedly listed it among the most frequent sunscreen allergens.

paras: It was formulated into sunscreens as one of several filters. Protection is cumulative, so any visible difference in wrinkles and tone shows up over years of regular sun protection rather than weeks. It is not a common ingredient in current routines.

Contact allergy and photoallergy are its main documented problem. Patch-test series found roughly 5 to 7.5% of tested patients reacting to sunscreens overall, with mexenone among the leading culprits. People with a history of reacting to oxybenzone or other benzophenones are the ones most likely to be affected. Its current regulatory status was not documented.

angle.text: Mexenone is an older sunscreen filter that absorbs UV so less sun damage reaches your skin, which slows sun-driven wrinkling and uneven tone over the years. It is known more from dermatology allergy clinics than from current skincare routines.

lead: Mexenone (benzophenone-10, trade name Uvistat) is a benzophenone-derived sunscreening agent with the chemical name (2-hydroxy-4-methoxyphenyl)(4-methylphenyl)methanone (C15H14O3).[1] It is chemically related to oxybenzone (benzophenone-3).[2]

It is mainly known in the medical literature as a contact and photocontact allergen. Patch-test series from clinics in the 1980s and 1990s repeatedly reported mexenone as one of the most frequent sunscreen sensitisers.[3][4] Little else about its performance as a cosmetic ingredient is documented in the sources reviewed.

paras: Mexenone has a molar mass of about 242 g/mol and is one of the numbered benzophenone sunscreen agents.[1] Wikipedia's entry is a stub and does not give its absorption range or regulatory status.[1]

In a 1987 report from a UK contact dermatitis clinic, 15 of 280 patients (5%) tested with sunscreens reacted, and mexenone was the most frequent allergen (six patients).[3] A 1993 study of 214 patients with photosensitivity disorders or polymorphic light eruption, and controls, found 16 (7.5%) reacting to at least one sunscreen; benzophenones (mexenone and oxybenzone) accounted for 8 of 27 positive patch tests.[4] A 1980 case report described mexenone allergy that presented as a flare of light sensitivity,[5] and a 1991 paper examined contact and photocontact allergy to oxybenzone and mexenone.[2]
Studies of photopatch testing set the UV-A dose needed to provoke responses in people already sensitised to agents including mexenone, oxybenzone and isopropyl dibenzoylmethane.[6]

Human studies of mexenone are patch-test and photopatch-test series in dermatology clinics rather than trials of sun protection. These report mexenone as a leading cause of sunscreen allergy in the clinics studied, with sensitisation in roughly 5 to 7.5% of patients tested with sunscreen series in the 1987 and 1993 reports.[3][4] A 2006 Colombian series of photoallergic contact dermatitis also listed sunscreen causes among its findings.[7]
A 1975 paper surveyed chemical light-screening agents of the time.[8] No community discussion of mexenone in looksmaxxing forums was found.
